Can a model tell when a risk is worth taking?

And when does playing safe cost more?

Models play backgammon, and an engine scores every move they make. We measure whether each risk a model takes is the right one, and what that costs. Every decision is public.

Hit risk only: being hit. Gammon risk and priming are not in it.

Setups met different positions; risk judgement is not adjusted for how hard they were. Paired comparisons wait for the shared positions.

Big risks found: stake above 0.08. Big needless risks: the chosen play lost more than 0.08.

‡ Risks with a probability: decisions whose plays were split into groups have no single probability and are left out; their count is shown per row. Setups that return no probabilities show N/A. Confidence on the call: ranking score only, no calibration gap (the probability is for the chosen play, not the risk). Definitions

Ability, caution and the SDT reference: A simple model of the risk call (equal-variance signal detection); setups met different positions. The cost-derived SDT reference uses the setup's own mean equity lost per needless and per missed risk; those costs depend on the setup's own play, so it is a reference under that model, not the best caution, and a correctly classified call can still lose equity. Rates corrected by adding 0.5 to the counts and 1 to the totals; a setup without Risk pays or Safety pays decisions shows N/A. Intervals: 95%, blocks of two seat-swapped games resampled. Definitions

The same at the 0.02 margin (robustness)

Hit risk only: being hit. Gammon risk and priming are not in it.

Setups met different positions; risk judgement is not adjusted for how hard they were. Paired comparisons wait for the shared positions.

Big risks found: stake above 0.08. Big needless risks: the chosen play lost more than 0.08.

‡ Risks with a probability: decisions whose plays were split into groups have no single probability and are left out; their count is shown per row. Setups that return no probabilities show N/A. Confidence on the call: ranking score only, no calibration gap (the probability is for the chosen play, not the risk). Definitions

Ability, caution and the SDT reference: A simple model of the risk call (equal-variance signal detection); setups met different positions. The cost-derived SDT reference uses the setup's own mean equity lost per needless and per missed risk; those costs depend on the setup's own play, so it is a reference under that model, not the best caution, and a correctly classified call can still lose equity. Rates corrected by adding 0.5 to the counts and 1 to the totals; a setup without Risk pays or Safety pays decisions shows N/A. Intervals: 95%, blocks of two seat-swapped games resampled. Definitions

Hit risk only: being hit. Gammon risk and priming are not in it.

Setups met different positions; risk judgement is not adjusted for how hard they were. Paired comparisons wait for the shared positions.

Big risks found: stake above 0.08. Big needless risks: the chosen play lost more than 0.08.

‡ Risks with a probability: decisions whose plays were split into groups have no single probability and are left out; their count is shown per row. Setups that return no probabilities show N/A. Confidence on the call: ranking score only, no calibration gap (the probability is for the chosen play, not the risk). Definitions

Ability, caution and the SDT reference: A simple model of the risk call (equal-variance signal detection); setups met different positions. The cost-derived SDT reference uses the setup's own mean equity lost per needless and per missed risk; those costs depend on the setup's own play, so it is a reference under that model, not the best caution, and a correctly classified call can still lose equity. Rates corrected by adding 0.5 to the counts and 1 to the totals; a setup without Risk pays or Safety pays decisions shows N/A. Intervals: 95%, blocks of two seat-swapped games resampled. Definitions

§ list-price estimate; runs on our GPUs · † plays split into groups · Not measured: no value recorded. Method

Setups played different positions; league comparisons are not paired.

Risk pays vs safety pays

  • League 1: model setups found 19% to 45% of the risks that paid, and played safe in 60% to 92% of the positions where safety paid.
  • League 2: model setups found 25% to 46% of the risks that paid, and played safe in 83% to 98% of the positions where safety paid.
  • League 3: model setups found 30% to 56% of the risks that paid, and played safe in 89% to 98% of the positions where safety paid.

Can a model predict where it will waver?

Stage B: five teams

Close choices: does a setup know where it hesitates?

Scope. Gemma 4 31B (on) was started but not completed: two reboots and a GPU fault interrupted it, and it was stopped after 311 of 500 play calls on 2026-10-25. Its partial data is not reported.

Each team answered the same 100 positions 5 times, and once more in a separate call naming the features it expects to differ between the plays it might choose (hitting risk, making a point, the race, the prime). Observed set: the features that differ between any of the 5 chosen plays. Primary score: exact agreement of the predicted set with the observed set. Secondary score, declared secondary: partial overlap of the two sets. Baseline: the team's own predictions shuffled within phase, 1,000 seeded shuffles; p = the share of shuffles scoring at least the observed mean. Stage B asks again and looks at repeated answers; it is separate from stage A (Confidence tab), which reads recorded league decisions.

Not a ranking: each team is compared with its own shuffled baseline, never with another team. Rows are in fixed alphabetical order and the table cannot be sorted.

A change, or no change, across five answers doesn't measure the model's whole behaviour.

Against its baseline: above the range = the observed mean is above the baseline's 97.5% point. Inside the range = not clearly above the baseline; a result that is not significant is not evidence that the team equals its baseline.

Most positions have no changed feature: the five answers chose the same play (71–92 positions per team), or changed play without changing a feature. So much of each score comes from predicting “none” where the team does not hesitate.

No team gave the same play in all five answers on every scored position.

Every team kept its league settings. Temperature: the value sent or the provider's documented default where known, otherwise not disclosed.
